chapters.title: The Demo Always Works
chapters.tease: A demo shows the system can succeed. Only an eval shows how often it actually does.

chapters.title: Vibes Are a Sample of Five
chapters.tease: A vibe is a measurement with the sample size, the selection and the bias left out. Treat it as a hypothesis.

chapters.title: Non-Determinism Is Not an Excuse
chapters.tease: Outputs that vary have a success rate, and rates can be measured. Variation is the reason to measure.

chapters.title: The Anatomy of an Eval
chapters.tease: Every eval has four parts: inputs, the system under test, a grader and a score. Name all four.

chapters.title: Benchmarks Are Someone Else's Opinion
chapters.tease: A leaderboard tells you who is good at the test. Only your own eval tells you who is good at your job.

chapters.title: You Are Testing a System
chapters.tease: Users never meet your model alone. They meet everything you wrapped around it, so evaluate the whole system.

chapters.title: The Eval You Can Run Today
chapters.tease: Your first eval is a twenty-row spreadsheet: input, output, verdict and one sentence on why.

chapters.title: Read the Outputs First
chapters.tease: Before choosing any metric, read a hundred outputs. Error analysis tells you which questions to ask.

chapters.title: Who Owns Quality
chapters.tease: Quality is not one person's job, but each part of it belongs to someone. Name who owns which part.

chapters.title: An Opinion, Written Down
chapters.tease: An eval is not an objective instrument. It is an opinion about quality, written down precisely.

chapters.title: Start From the User's Job
chapters.tease: Measure whether the user got what they came for, not whether the answer was merely fluent and polite.

chapters.title: Good, Bad and Unacceptable
chapters.tease: Sort outcomes into four tiers. An average hides the one failure that should stop a release.

chapters.title: Turning Taste Into Criteria
chapters.tease: Taste that lives only in heads cannot be applied by a grader. Turn it into criteria, starting from examples.

chapters.title: Specific Beats Ambitious
chapters.tease: Helpful, accurate and safe commits to nothing. Rewrite each goal so two people would reach the same verdict.

chapters.title: Many Goals, One Dashboard
chapters.tease: Quality, speed, cost and safety pull against each other. Maximise one inside hard limits on the others.

chapters.title: Reference Answers and Their Limits
chapters.tease: A reference answer is one good answer, not the only one. On open tasks, turn it into a checklist of key facts.

chapters.title: When There Is No Right Answer
chapters.tease: Open tasks have no key, but still have wrong answers. Enforce a floor, then compare for quality.

chapters.title: Guardrail Metrics
chapters.tease: Every change targets one metric. Guardrails are the numbers that must not get worse while you chase it.

chapters.title: The One-Page Eval Spec
chapters.tease: A one-page spec says what the eval measures, what it ignores and how to read it. Code alone cannot.

chapters.title: Criteria That Age Well
chapters.tease: Criteria written at launch drift from what users care about. Review them quarterly, and retire as well as add.

chapters.title: The Dataset Is the Spec
chapters.tease: Whatever is not in the eval dataset is, in practice, not required. The dataset is the real spec.

chapters.title: Golden Sets, Small and Trusted
chapters.tease: A small, expert-checked golden set that everyone trusts is worth more than a large one you must argue with.

chapters.title: Sampling From Production
chapters.tease: Your logs hold the best eval data. Sample randomly to measure quality, and on purpose to find problems.

chapters.title: Stratify or Be Fooled
chapters.tease: An overall score can look healthy while one important slice fails badly. Report scores per slice.

chapters.title: Synthetic Data on a Leash
chapters.tease: Synthetic data widens coverage but sounds tidier than real users. Constrain it and keep a human leash.

chapters.title: Hard Cases and the Long Tail
chapters.tease: Once a system works, common cases stop being informative. Collect hard cases and score them apart.

chapters.title: Labelling Without Losing Your Mind
chapters.tease: Inconsistent labels measure labellers' moods. Guidelines, a pilot and a rulings log keep them steady.

chapters.title: Contamination and Leakage
chapters.tease: If test examples leak into prompts, training or the index, scores rise while real ability does not.

chapters.title: Version the Dataset
chapters.tease: A score means nothing without its dataset version. Version data and grader, and record both every run.

chapters.title: Every Bug Becomes a Test
chapters.tease: Every real failure becomes a test before the fix. Then it stays, so the same bug rarely surprises you twice.

chapters.title: The Grader Is Half the Eval
chapters.tease: The grader is half the experiment. Use the cheapest grader that can reliably judge each criterion.

chapters.title: Exact Match and Its Discontents
chapters.tease: Exact match suits one-answer tasks. Elsewhere it grades formatting, so normalise or structure output.

chapters.title: Code-Based Checks
chapters.tease: Many criteria can be checked by ordinary code: fast, free, consistent, and precise about why it failed.

chapters.title: Execution as a Grader
chapters.tease: For executable outputs, the best grader runs them. It accepts every correct form and catches subtle bugs.

chapters.title: Similarity Scores and Their Blind Spots
chapters.tease: Similarity scores notice change, not truth. A confident near-miss can score just like the right answer.

chapters.title: Rubrics a Grader Can Follow
chapters.tease: Rate for quality invites everyone's own idea. Write narrow criteria with pass, fail and edge examples.

chapters.title: Pass or Fail Beats One to Ten
chapters.tease: One-to-ten scales drift between graders and days. Binary checks agree more often and tell you what to fix.

chapters.title: Human Review Done Properly
chapters.tease: Human review is the gold standard only when it has guidelines, blinding, sensible sampling and adjudication.

chapters.title: Measuring the Humans
chapters.tease: Measure how often your human reviewers agree. If they cannot agree, the eval measures which human you asked.

chapters.title: Grading the Grader
chapters.tease: Every automated grader makes systematic mistakes. Compare it with human labels and trust it only that far.

chapters.title: Why Models Mark Homework
chapters.tease: Model judges read language at scale, but bring opinions you did not choose. Trust them only once measured.

chapters.title: Writing a Judge Prompt
chapters.tease: A judge reads literally and cannot ask questions. Brief it with task, criterion, edges and format.

chapters.title: Pairwise or Pointwise
chapters.tease: Ask whether it is good when you know what good is. Ask which is better when you only know it when you see it.

chapters.title: The Order Effect
chapters.tease: Judges often favour whichever answer they see first or second. Judge every pair in both orders.

chapters.title: Long Answers Look Clever
chapters.tease: Judges prefer long, confident, well-formatted answers. Left alone, they train your system to look busy.

chapters.title: Family Resemblance
chapters.tease: A judge may favour outputs that resemble its own. Use mixed judges and a human sample when choosing models.

chapters.title: Calibrate Against Humans
chapters.tease: Calibration measures a judge against human labels and improves it until it is fit for purpose. Do not skip it.

chapters.title: Give the Judge a Reference
chapters.tease: Without a reference, a judge grades plausibility. Give it the facts as a checklist, and it grades truth.

chapters.title: Reasoning First, Verdict Last
chapters.tease: Ask the judge to reason through each criterion before its verdict. Then the verdict follows the evidence.

chapters.title: When Not to Use a Judge
chapters.tease: A judge is the costliest, least transparent automated grader. Use it only where judgement is truly needed.

chapters.title: A Score Is an Estimate
chapters.tease: An eval score is an estimate from a sample, so every headline number needs its margin beside it.

chapters.title: Three Sources of Wobble
chapters.tease: Scores wobble for three reasons: the sample, the system's randomness and the grader. Each has its own fix.

chapters.title: Confidence Intervals for the Rest of Us
chapters.tease: An interval says how much to believe a score; a rule of thumb or a bootstrap gets you one.

chapters.title: How Many Examples Is Enough
chapters.tease: Sample size follows the smallest difference you must detect; halving the margin takes four times the data.

chapters.title: Compare on the Same Items
chapters.tease: Run both versions on the same examples: only the items where they disagree tell you which is better.

chapters.title: Repeated Runs and pass@k
chapters.tease: pass@k asks if any attempt succeeds; pass^k asks if every one does. Pick the one your users live in.

chapters.title: Averages That Lie
chapters.tease: An average can fall while every slice underneath improves, because the mix of examples changed.

chapters.title: Significant Is Not Important
chapters.tease: Significance says a difference is probably real. Whether it matters is a judgement you make in advance.

chapters.title: The Garden of Forking Paths
chapters.tease: Try enough things and some look like wins by chance. Explore on dev data, then confirm once on held-out data.

chapters.title: Reporting Results Honestly
chapters.tease: Most misleading eval reports are not dishonest, just incomplete. A seven-part template fixes that.

chapters.title: Evaluate the Parts, Then the Whole
chapters.tease: End-to-end scores say something went wrong; component evals say what. You need both.

chapters.title: Retrieval Has Its Own Scorecard
chapters.tease: Score retrieval on its own with labelled passages: if the answer was never retrieved, no prompt can fix it.

chapters.title: Faithfulness and Groundedness
chapters.tease: Faithfulness asks whether every claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved context, one claim at a time.

chapters.title: Citations You Can Check
chapters.tease: Check every citation twice: does the source exist in the context, and does it actually support the claim?

chapters.title: When the Answer Is Not There
chapters.tease: Add questions your sources cannot answer, and score both honest abstention and wrongful refusal.

chapters.title: Tool Calls Are Testable
chapters.tease: A tool call is a structured decision, so test the choice of tool, its arguments and how the result is used.

chapters.title: Trajectories Versus Outcomes
chapters.tease: Judge the outcome first, then check the trajectory for alarming routes and lucky guesses.

chapters.title: Environments for Agents
chapters.tease: To test an agent that acts, build an isolated, resettable world for it, then check the final state.

chapters.title: Long Tasks and Partial Credit
chapters.tease: Break long agent tasks into milestones, so you can see how far each run got and where runs stall.

chapters.title: Simulated Users and Many Turns
chapters.tease: Conversations need a partner: simulate users with personas and goals, then grade the whole transcript.

chapters.title: The Regression Suite
chapters.tease: A regression suite guards the behaviours that must not break: core tasks, past failures and critical cases.

chapters.title: Evals in CI
chapters.tease: Put evals in CI in tiers: fast checks on every change, the full suite nightly, the costly tier before release.

chapters.title: Thresholds and Flaky Failures
chapters.tease: Set gate tolerances from measured noise, and fix flaky examples by cause, or people learn to ignore red.

chapters.title: Changing Models Without Fear
chapters.tease: A model upgrade is just another change: run the same suite and apply a decision rule written in advance.

chapters.title: Prompts Are Code
chapters.tease: Prompts change behaviour as much as code, so version them, review them with evals and deploy them alike.

chapters.title: Online Evaluation
chapters.tease: Online evals grade a sample of live traffic after users are served, catching what offline sets missed.

chapters.title: Signals From Real Users
chapters.tease: User behaviour is a constant quality signal, but explicit feedback is sparse and implicit signals are proxies.

chapters.title: A/B Tests for Probabilistic Products
chapters.tease: An A/B test shows what a change does to users, if you gate it offline, split by user and decide in advance.

chapters.title: Watching for Drift
chapters.tease: Quality drifts with no code change, as inputs, context and models move. Each kind needs its own watch.

chapters.title: Closing the Loop
chapters.tease: Production failures become examples, examples improve datasets and gates, and evals stay close to reality.

chapters.title: Safety Is a Quality Dimension
chapters.tease: Harmful advice is not a quality system with a safety problem. It is low quality where it matters most.

chapters.title: Threat Models Before Test Cases
chapters.tease: Before collecting adversarial prompts, map what you protect, from whom and how harm could happen.

chapters.title: Red-Teaming by Hand
chapters.tease: Human red teamers probe, escalate and combine tricks until a gap opens, and every success becomes a test.

chapters.title: Automated Adversaries
chapters.tease: An attacker model generates and refines attacks at scale, and every success joins the safety regression suite.

chapters.title: Prompt Injection Tests
chapters.tease: Plant instructions in everything your system reads, then check with code whether it obeyed them.

chapters.title: Over-Refusal Is Also Failure
chapters.tease: Refusing legitimate requests is a failure too; an eval that only measures harm pushes systems towards it.

chapters.title: Privacy and Leakage
chapters.tease: Whatever a system can see, it can be persuaded to say. Filter by permission first, then test with canaries.

chapters.title: Fairness Lives in the Slices
chapters.tease: A system can excel on average while one group quietly gets worse answers. Slices and counterfactuals find it.

chapters.title: Agents With Sharp Tools
chapters.tease: Rank every agent tool by the harm it can do, and test what the agent does when overstepping is tempting.

chapters.title: Safety Gates That Ship
chapters.tease: A safety gate names a suite and a threshold; only severe, well-tested risks should block a release.

chapters.title: What Evals Cost
chapters.tease: Evals cost compute, people and time. Not having them costs the same money later, with interest.

chapters.title: Cheap Evals First
chapters.tease: Layer graders from cheap to costly: code checks on everything, judges on a sample, people on a few.

chapters.title: Tooling Without Lock-In
chapters.tease: Use evaluation tools freely, but keep datasets, rubrics, graders and results in open formats you own.

chapters.title: The Weekly Eval Review
chapters.tease: A 45-minute weekly review turns eval results into steady small decisions, not occasional emergencies.

chapters.title: Everybody's Job, Somebody's Name
chapters.tease: Evals work when everyone participates and one named person is accountable. Without either, they decay.

chapters.title: Goodhart Comes for Everyone
chapters.tease: When a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring. Watch for eval scores rising while users stay flat.

chapters.title: When Users and Evals Disagree
chapters.tease: When users and evals disagree, investigate: each pattern of disagreement points to a specific fix.

chapters.title: Evals as Documentation
chapters.tease: A well-kept eval is the most precise documentation of what an AI product should do, case by case.

chapters.title: Taste Still Matters
chapters.tease: Measurement cannot tell you what to want. Taste notices what passing outputs lack; evals check it.

chapters.title: An Eval Is an Opinion About Quality
chapters.tease: An eval is a written-down opinion about quality, precise enough to run, argue with and improve.
